insider_note: The equation has dx and dy mixed with the unknown x appearing without a derivative attached, which is the signal that this is linear IN x, not in y — write it as dx/dy + P(y)x = Q(y) rather than trying to force it into the usual dy/dx form.

steps.label: Rewrite as linear in x and identify P
steps.margin_note: One mark. The x term appears without a derivative, so divide by (1+y²) and treat this as linear in x with y as the free variable.
steps.memory_tip: When x sits alone (not as dx/dy) alongside a dy term, the equation is linear in x, solved with y as the independent variable.
lines: This is in the form dx/dy + xP(y) = Q(y),
which is linear D.E in x.
steps.why: Because x appears without a derivative next to a dy term, the equation is naturally linear in x rather than in y, so it is rewritten as dx/dy + Px = Q with y playing the role x usually plays.
common_mistakes: Trying to force this into a dy/dx = … linear-in-y form, which does not work because x is not isolated the same way.
Losing the minus sign on x when dividing (Tan⁻¹y − x) by (1 + y²).

steps.label: Find the integrating factor
steps.margin_note: One mark. I.F. = e^(∫P dy), the same formula as before but integrated with respect to y.
steps.memory_tip: The formula for the integrating factor never changes — only the variable of integration switches to y here.
steps.why: The integrating-factor formula applies identically whether the equation is linear in x or in y — only the variable being integrated changes, from x to y.
common_mistakes: Writing e^(Tan⁻¹x) by mistake, confusing this with the earlier answer 98 which used Tan⁻¹x.
Forgetting the e^(...) wrapper and leaving the I.F. as Tan⁻¹y.

steps.label: Set up the integral and substitute
steps.margin_note: One mark. x·(I.F.) = ∫(I.F.)Q dy is the same formula as before, with x and y swapped.
steps.memory_tip: t = Tan⁻¹y makes dt = dy/(1+y²) exactly, matching the leftover factor in the integral.
lines: Hence the solution is x·(I.F.) = ∫(I.F.)Q dy
Put Tan⁻¹y = t ⇒ 1/(1 + y²) dy = dt,
steps.why: Multiplying Q by the integrating factor and substituting t = Tan⁻¹y turns the integral into ∫t eᵗ dt, since dt is exactly the 1/(1+y²)dy factor already present in the integrand.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that Tan⁻¹y appears twice — once inside the exponential and once as the plain factor t multiplying it.
Missing that dt = dy/(1+y²) is the exact leftover factor, and trying to substitute something else.

steps.label: Integrate by parts and finish
steps.margin_note: The last mark. ∫teᵗdt = eᵗ(t − 1) + c is a standard integration-by-parts result.
steps.memory_tip: Integration by parts on t·eᵗ always gives eᵗ(t − 1) — worth memorising as a standard pair.
lines: ∫t·eᵗ dt = teᵗ − ∫eᵗ dt = teᵗ − eᵗ + c = eᵗ(t − 1) + c
and putting t = Tan⁻¹y back in:
steps.why: Integration by parts on t·eᵗ gives the standard result eᵗ(t − 1); dividing the whole equation by eᵗ afterwards isolates x and, substituting t = Tan⁻¹y back in, gives the final answer with a negative exponential term for the arbitrary constant.
common_mistakes: Choosing the wrong parts for integration by parts, taking eᵗ as the part to differentiate instead of t.
Forgetting to divide the constant term c by eᵗ as well, and leaving it as +c·eᵗ instead of +c·e^(−Tan⁻¹y).
